source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (Table 3, intrinsic rounds)
finding: With no oracle label, asking the model to review its own answer lowered accuracy in every setting, and more rounds lowered it more. Most of the damage was correct answers changed to wrong ones.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 (round 2) -> 74.7 (round 3); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CSQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. Table 2 oracle-stop numbers (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3; GPT-4 95.5 -> 97.5) show the loss comes from not knowing when to stop.
limits: GPT-3.5/GPT-4 (2023 endpoints), no reasoning models. Not a token-matched test of a review step against extra samples. Not evidence about 2025-26 frontier models.
agent_relevance: Baseline for gap 2: the review step must be gated by an external or trace signal, never fired blindly. Old models only; re-test on current models.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024, TACL) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey (abstract and intro re-read for gap 3)
finding: Survey finding in four parts: no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM (with one narrow exception whose wording was cut in the text extract); self-correction works well where reliable external feedback exists; large-scale fine-tuning can enable it; some tasks have properties that suit it. The bottleneck is the feedback, not the revision.
numbers: Qualitative survey. No pooled effect size.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey ends mid-2024. Does not cover reasoning models trained with RL. The abstract extraction was partly interleaved, so the exception clause is not quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: tells the agent to look for signals that make checking easier than solving (tests, tools, re-derivation) and to skip review where none exist.

source: Olausson et al. (2024, ICLR) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Self-repair with unit-test output, compared with plain extra samples at the SAME sample budget, gives small, uneven gains and sometimes none. The weak part is the model's feedback on its own code. A stronger model or a human writing the feedback helps clearly.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples + 1 repair each (20 total) gives pass rate 1.05x pass@20 without repair; gains up to 8% over baseline at best. GPT-3.5 on APPS: marginal gains only at the largest budgets; up to 34% relative gain on competition-level problems. Replacing GPT-4's own explanations with a human programmer's raised repaired-program pass fraction from 33.3% to 52.6% (1.58x). Some configurations fell below baseline (0.97x of pass@22).
limits: Code only, 2023 models (Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4-0314). Unit tests exist in this setting, yet the self-feedback step still limits it. Small human study.
agent_relevance: Strongest token-matched control for gaps 9 and 3: a cheap external signal (tests) is not enough; spend budget on diverse first attempts before repair. Add an equal-sample baseline to every review test.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Sequential revisions versus parallel best-of-N at equal compute: which wins depends on question difficulty. Easy questions favour sequential revision; hard questions favour parallel resampling or tree search. A difficulty-adaptive policy matched best-of-N with about 4x less compute.
numbers: PaLM 2-S* on MATH. Compute-optimal allocation beats best-of-N using about 4x less computation (both revisions and PRM search). FLOPs-matched against a 14x larger model: test-time compute preferable on easy and intermediate questions, little benefit on the hardest.
limits: Uses a fine-tuned revision model and a trained verifier/PRM, not a prompt-only review. 2024 model, MATH only. Difficulty was estimated from verifier scores.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 9: one fixed review/stop rule cannot be best on all items. The trigger should include a difficulty estimate: revise on easy items, restart or branch on hard ones.

source: Tsui (2025, COLM 2026 v3) Self-Correction Bench: the self-correction blind spot in LLMs (frontier rows and Wait table)
finding: Models fix an error when it is shown as someone else's text but not when it sits in their own output. The v3 paper adds closed models and on-policy errors. Appending 'Wait' to a non-reasoning model recovers most of the gap to its reasoning twin.
numbers: Average blind spot 64.5% over 14 open non-reasoning models; Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%; 62.8% on non-math BIG-Bench Mistake tasks. On models' own real (on-policy) errors, only 4.3%-10.8% were caught once shown externally. 'Wait' cut the blind spot 89.3% on average. Table 3 mean accuracy, base / +Wait / reasoning twin: DeepSeek-V3 0.567/0.902/0.908; phi-4 0.325/0.701/0.707; Qwen3-14B 0.117/0.868/0.843; Qwen3-32B 0.045/0.793/0.894; Qwen3-235B 0.328/0.856/0.876.
quote: Appending "Wait" requires no training yet reduces the blind spot by 89.3%
limits: Errors are injected by prefill in simple tasks (shuffled objects, logical deduction), not natural long agent traces. Only two closed models, because few APIs support prefill. Reasoning models serve as the comparison, not as test subjects at frontier level. No token-matched control: Wait also lengthens output.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: supports a 'Wait'/colleague framing cue inside S6 for non-reasoning backbones. Unknown whether it helps current reasoning models or long traces; test with an equal-length filler cue as control.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs (re-read for stop-rule numbers)
finding: In more than 92% of cases the first solution round already holds the correct answer; later rounds mostly repeat it. Shortening the later rounds saves tokens without losing accuracy on easy and medium sets.
numbers: Tokens for '2+3': o1-like models used 1,953% more than conventional models. First-round correct share above 92% overall (figure shows 97% on ASDIV and about 89-93% on MATH500 depending on model). Shortening method cut output 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview with accuracy kept.
limits: Gains measured on ASDIV, GSM8K, MATH500; harder sets (GPQA, AIME) show smaller gains. The first-answer split is LLM-judged. Later rounds help on hard items, so the rule is difficulty-dependent.
agent_relevance: Gap 5, overthinking half: S6 should stop after the first answer passes a check on easy items. Needs a difficulty gate to avoid cutting useful checks on hard items.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: on the underthinking of o1-like LLMs (Tables 1 and 3)
finding: Wrong answers contain more thought switches than right ones on hard math, so switching is a trace feature that goes with error. A decoding penalty on switch tokens (TIP) gives small accuracy gains with no model tuning. A prompt asking the model to stay on one path barely helped.
numbers: Underthinking score (token waste in wrong answers): QwQ-32B-Preview 58.2 on MATH500-Hard, 48.3 GPQA, 65.0 AIME24; DeepSeek-R1-671B 65.4 MATH500-Hard, 58.8 GPQA. TIP Pass@1: QwQ AIME24 38.3 -> 44.1; GPQA 57.6 -> 59.1; MATH500-Hard 83.1 -> 83.7; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B AIME24 61.4 -> 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 AIME24 73.8 -> 74.8 (with prompt only: 72.4).
limits: Open o1-like models of 2025 only, math and GPQA. TIP needs decoding access. Pass@1 gains of 0.6 to 5.8 points with large run-to-run spread (32 samples). Correlation of switches with error does not prove fewer switches cause better answers.
agent_relevance: Gap 5, underthinking half: a switch counter is a cheap trace trigger. It pulls opposite to the overthinking fix ('stop earlier'), so the trigger must tell the two cases apart.

source: Hassid et al. (2026 v2) Don't overthink it: preferring shorter thinking chains for improved LLM reasoning
finding: For the same question, shorter sampled reasoning chains are more often right than the longest. Running k chains in parallel and stopping at the first m to finish (short-m@k) matched or beat majority voting with fewer thinking tokens.
numbers: Up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest chain for the same question; short-1@k up to 40% fewer thinking tokens than majority voting at low compute; short-3@k beats majority voting at all budgets, up to 33% wall-time cut.
limits: Open reasoning models; math benchmarks. Chain length is a trace feature but not a stop rule inside a single trace. It selects among samples, not a review of a trace in flight.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 5: a finish-first signal across independent samples is a free, equal-token alternative to a self-question trigger. Good control arm.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning models can be effective without thinking
finding: Skipping the thinking phase (prefill an empty think block) beats full thinking at equal token budget, most clearly at small budgets. Parallel NoThinking samples with a verifier or confidence pick approach full thinking at far lower latency.
numbers: ACM23: 51.3 NoThinking vs 28.9 Thinking at 700 tokens. Parallel NoThinking is comparable to Thinking with up to 9x longer latency (abstract). Seven datasets: math, theorem proving, coding.
limits: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models. Token-controlled mainly at low budgets; at large budgets Thinking catches up on many tasks. Gain depends on a verifier or confidence selector.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a strong equal-token control. Any claim that a metacognitive structure helps must beat extra short parallel samples at the same cost.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic early exit in reasoning models (DEER)
finding: At each reasoning transition word, force a trial answer and exit when the model's token confidence in it is high. No training. Shorter traces and slightly higher accuracy across 11 reasoning models and 10 benchmarks.
numbers: CoT length cut by 19.1% to 80.1% on average; accuracy change +0.3% to +5.0% (abstract). In Meta-R1's Table 1, DEER on R1-Distill-Qwen-14B: avg accuracy 84.9 vs vanilla 84.0, tokens 4,690 vs 5,691; AIME24 70.0 vs 64.4.
limits: Needs logit access for the confidence. Open reasoning models; math, GPQA and code. Not compared with a prompted self-question.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 5: a training-free stop trigger built from a model-internal signal at answer points. Our agent can mimic it with 'state the current answer and check agreement' at step boundaries.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning models know when they're right: probing hidden states for self-verification
finding: A small probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct, is well calibrated, and also predicts correctness of future answers. Used as an exit trigger it cut tokens with no accuracy loss.
numbers: In-distribution ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1 on the benchmarks tested; probe-based early exit cut inference tokens by 24% without lowering accuracy.
limits: Needs open weights and a trained probe per model; out-of-distribution results are weaker than in-distribution. Reasoning-distilled models only. Not usable by an API-only agent.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: internal and trace signals carry correctness information, in line with the human online-over-offline gap. Cannot be copied by a prompt-only scaffold.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep think with confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Token-level confidence of a trace (lowest group confidence) is used to drop weak traces during or after generation. Confidence-weighted voting beats plain majority voting, and online stopping of low-confidence traces saves most of the tokens.
numbers: Offline: DeepConf@512 99.9% on AIME 2025 with GPT-OSS-120B (no tools) vs 97.0% majority vote (cons@512) vs 91.8% pass@1. Online: up to 84.7% fewer generated tokens than full parallel thinking, accuracy kept or raised. Models: DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-8B/32B, GPT-OSS-20B/120B; 64 repetitions per setting.
limits: Needs logprobs. Gains depend on running many parallel traces (up to 512). Math and GPQA-style benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 5, 8: a trace-confidence trigger works at equal or lower token cost than majority voting. An API agent without logprobs can approximate it with agreement among cheap samples.

source: Dong et al. (2025) Meta-R1 (Table 1, ablation, small meta-level)
finding: A small separate model (Qwen2.5-1.5B or 3B instruct) monitors the reasoning of a larger model and injects advice when token-type frequencies in the last chunk cross a threshold. Removing the online regulation stage costs the most. No arm lets the large model monitor itself.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-14B averages: vanilla acc 84.0 at 5,691 tokens; DEER 84.9 at 4,690; Meta-R1 87.0 at 3,941. AIME24 64.4 -> 70.0. 32B: Meta-R1 variants avg 88.2-89.5 at about 3,300-3,600 tokens vs 82.9 (greedy) at 3,556. Scaling the meta model beyond 1.5B-3B gave small gains for 14-19% more tokens; 14B gave +0.1 for 18.6% more tokens.
limits: Only GSM8K, AIME2024, MATH500 and two R1-Distill backbones, run by the authors. No independent replication found. The monitor works from frequency features and logit control, so it is not a plain prompt scaffold. Row labels for Meta-R1 versus Meta-R1 Pro are ambiguous in the text extract.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. Part of the gain comes from a trace-feature trigger (token frequencies), which supports a 'trace over self-question' direction, but the same-model self-monitor control is missing.

source: Gou et al. (2024, ICLR) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing (with-tool vs without-tool rows)
finding: Revising after checking the output with a tool (search, code interpreter) improves QA and math. The same loop without the tool gives much less, and on some rows no better than the starting answer.
limits: Which model each row block belongs to is not clear from the text extract. 2023 models. Tools are search and code runners; tasks without such a tool are not covered. Self-consistency (a sample-matched comparison) is about equal to w/o Tool.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a tool check is the signal that makes review pay. Tasks with no tool (open design, puzzles without a checker) should skip S6 review or use re-derivation.

source: Swanson (1990) Influence of metacognitive knowledge and aptitude on problem solving (gap 7 retry)
finding: Still not opened. The APA page returned HTTP 403. Crossref lists the paper (271 citing works indexed) but holds no abstract. WebSearch, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were out of budget in this pass, so no replication or prompt-only version was found.
numbers: None verified. Crossref cited-by count 271 at the 2026-11-01 lookup.
limits: This is a gap-search failure, not evidence for or against compensation.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'metacognition compensates for low ability' in the agent design until the paper is read.

source: Synthesis of d05-d13: no study tests a self-question trigger against trace-feature triggers at equal tokens
finding: Every working stop or switch trigger found opens a trace or internal feature: trial-answer confidence (DEER), hidden-state probe (Zhang), group confidence (DeepConf), token-type frequency (Meta-R1), thought-switch count (Wang), chain length (Hassid). None is compared with a prompted self-question such as 'Is it getting me anywhere?'. Fixed-budget comparisons (NoThinking, s1 budget forcing in c14) are the only equal-token ones.
numbers: Six trigger families, 0 head-to-head with a prompted self-question. Token savings: 19.1-80.1% (DEER), 24% (probe), up to 84.7% (DeepConf), Meta-R1 tokens 15.7-32.7% lower (abstract wording).
limits: Based on what was opened in this pass. Search budget ran out, so other 2025-26 papers may exist.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open but the direction is clear: build the trigger from trace features; run the self-question as one arm only to test the human analogy.

source: Synthesis of d01, d03, d04, d09, d14: token-matched controls and review gains
finding: Where a token-matched sampling control was run, it often erased or exceeded the review gain: self-repair vs i.i.d. samples (d03), revision vs best-of-N depending on difficulty (d04), NoThinking vs Thinking at low budget (d09), self-consistency vs CRITIC w/o Tool (d14). No token-matched control was found for metacognitive prompting (Wang & Zhao) or Plan-and-Solve on current models.
numbers: Self-repair: 1.05x over pass@20 at best for GPT-4 on APPS. Sequential vs parallel: depends on difficulty; adaptive wins at about 4x less compute. NoThinking 51.3 vs 28.9 at 700 tokens.
limits: Mostly 2023-24 models and code or math. Absence of a matched control for metacognitive prompting is absence in what was opened, not proof it was never done.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: every claimed S6 gain in our own tests needs an equal-token extra-sample arm. Treat Plan-and-Solve and metacognitive-prompt gains as unproven for current models until measured that way.
